what_it_does: When many AI training jobs share a cluster of GPUs, each job typically locks in its plan for how to spread work across GPUs before it starts and never changes it, even as available resources shift. Rubick solves this by treating the training plan as something the cluster manager can swap on the fly, picking the best plan-plus-resource combination for every job continuously. On a 64-GPU cluster, Rubick cut average job completion time by up to 3.2x compared to the best prior systems.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Large model training offers many interchangeable plans for distributing work: split data across GPUs (data parallelism), split the model layers (pipeline parallelism), split individual math operations (tensor parallelism), offload weights to CPU memory, recompute intermediate values instead of storing them, and so on. Each plan makes very different demands on GPUs, CPUs, memory, and network bandwidth. Rubick's insight is that no single plan is best at all resource levels, and the cluster scheduler should be the one choosing and swapping plans as conditions change.

How it works. Rubick builds a mathematical performance model for each job — it predicts how fast a job will train under any given plan and any given resource allocation. The model has just seven tunable numbers, fitted from only seven short test runs. It accounts for how long the forward pass, backward pass, optimizer step, and inter-GPU communication each take, including how much of these can overlap in time. Once fitted, the model can predict speed for thousands of unseen plan-resource combinations instantly.

The key design choice. Rubick constructs a 'resource sensitivity curve' for each job: a graph of how much faster the job gets as you give it more GPUs or CPUs under its current best plan. The slope of this curve tells the scheduler exactly how much each unit of resource is worth to each job. The scheduler then reallocates continuously: it takes resources away from jobs with flat curves (low sensitivity) and gives them to jobs with steep curves (high sensitivity), maximizing total cluster output while still guaranteeing each guaranteed job at least its promised performance level.

The result. On a 64-GPU cluster with real training workloads, Rubick reduced average job completion time by 2.6–3.2x versus state-of-the-art fixed-plan schedulers. The reconfiguration cost was tiny: swapping plans averaged 78 seconds per job, only 1% of total GPU time.
